story: Georgian villagers were singing in parts before Christianity reached Georgia at the start of the 4th century. From the 7th and 8th centuries, Georgian church composers translated Greek Orthodox chants and added harmonies to the single-line melodies. Village singers, mostly farmers, kept the tradition going for centuries. In Kakheti, table songs set two soloists over a long drone bass; in Guria, three or four singers each took a separate line, with a yodel called krimanchuli. As farm work changed, the supra feast became where many kinds of song survived. The first professional choir, formed in 1886, began moving singers toward Western tuning. Under Soviet rule (1921–1991) church songs were forbidden, and huge regional choirs cut back the singers' improvising. In 1968 Anzor Erkomaishvili founded the Rustavi Choir; the Kakhetian song Chakrulo went into space on the Voyager records in 1977, and UNESCO listed Georgian polyphonic singing in 2001.
